paras: The lynching of Will Thomas was the hanging of a Black man by a band of about forty armed "regulators" at Tunnel Hill, Georgia, on the evening of March 9, 1888. Thomas was accused of assaulting Mrs. Eliza Anderson, a widow, the day before, and was hanged to a tree after she identified him. Papers across the country carried the Chattanooga dispatches, several stressing that the woman had asked to shoot him and been refused.

Tunnel Hill lay in north Georgia, given as twenty or twenty-five miles south of Chattanooga. According to a Chattanooga special of March 8, a Black man threw a blanket over the head of a widow named Anderson in her home that afternoon and ran off, and she said she could identify him. The same dispatch reported that "the town and county" were out with guns and pistols hunting him and predicted they would "make short work of him." Other reports described the act as a criminal assault, while the two Georgia papers called it an attempt to rape or "outrage" her.

A band of forty regulators armed with shotguns organized on the morning of March 9 and took up the pursuit. Accounts place the capture in the woods, at "Cohoutta" in Georgia, or nine miles north of Tunnel Hill near a place printed as "Capoatka," at about five o'clock that afternoon. He was brought back and taken before Mrs. Anderson, who identified him and, according to the wire report, asked for the privilege of shooting him, which was refused. The Savannah Morning News's Tunnel Hill correspondent wrote that he admitted at once that he was the man, and gave his home as Louisville, Kentucky.

The regulators then put a rope around his neck, mounted him on a mule and marched him through town. One version of the wire added that a band playing the dead march led the procession out of town. He was hanged to a tree on the outskirts about half an hour after his capture, at roughly 5:30 p.m.

According to the Memphis Appeal's special, the lynching was "conducted in good order" and the regulators went home saying they had done "a good day's work." No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The story moved from Chattanooga in at least three differently worded dispatches, and it ran on March 10 in New York, Washington, Memphis and Savannah. Through the following week it reappeared in Kentucky, Ohio, Tennessee, Virginia, South Carolina, Kansas and Minnesota, often as a one-sentence item in news summaries. The Minnesota summaries identified Mrs. Anderson as "a white woman," a detail absent from the original dispatches.

Southern papers took the mob's side openly: the Memphis Appeal headed its special "Verily, It Was Good Work," and the Louisville and Memphis texts called Thomas a "black brute." Northern and Washington papers printed the wire with little change under heads such as "Lynched by Regulators," "A Georgia Negro's Crime Speedily Punished" and "Southern Justice." Kentucky papers ran a shorter version as a "Lynching Bee," and an Emporia, Kansas, headline said the captors had reserved "the Right to Hang Him."

The National Republican of Washington alone named the man "William Thompson" and said he "was taken from jail and lynched by a mob," while the fuller dispatches describe a capture in the field by the regulators. The Tunnel Hill correspondent gave a third version, in which those holding him moved him away because his life was in danger before he was lynched that night. A later Minnesota summary dated the lynching March 10, but the March 9 dispatches and a Marietta report of "last Friday" agree on March 9.

reader.title: Lynching of Will Thomas
bases: A band of about forty armed 'regulators' hunted down, captured and hanged a Black man accused of assaulting a widow, without any legal process (A2, A6, A14).

Every account says Will Thomas was hanged to a tree by a band of forty regulators or a mob, with no court or officer involved, after the woman he was accused of assaulting identified him (A2, A6, A14); the papers framed it as punishment for the alleged crime (A3, A6).

At least three separately worded Chattanooga dispatches (A2/A3, A6/A10, A14) and a Tunnel Hill dispatch to the Savannah Morning News (A5) agree that Thomas was captured and lynched; the National Republican's jail version (A8) differs on custody but not on the killing.

accounts.label: Chattanooga wire (Sun version)
accounts.gist: Forty regulators traced Thomas to the woods and captured him, brought him before Mrs. Anderson, refused her request to shoot him, and hanged him to a tree after leading him out of town on a mule behind a band playing the dead march.

accounts.label: Chattanooga special (Memphis Appeal / Courier-Journal)
accounts.gist: Regulators organized the morning after the assault caught Thomas at Cohoutta at 5 o'clock, had him identified, marched him through town on a mule and hanged him, then said they had done a good day's work.

accounts.label: Tunnel Hill dispatch (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: He was captured nine miles north near 'Capoatka', was said to have admitted the act when confronted, and was moved away by those holding him because his life was in danger before he was lynched that night.

Northern and Washington papers ran the Chattanooga wire under heads such as 'Lynched by Regulators', 'A Negro Lynched' and 'Southern Justice', calling him 'the scoundrel' without comment of their own.

A band of forty self-styled 'regulators', also called a mob; no paper says they were deputized or led by officers.
Most accounts: captured in pursuit by the regulators; the National Republican alone says he was taken from jail.

Will Thomas (also 'William Thomas'; 'William Thompson' in one paper), described as colored or a negro, said to be from Louisville, Ky.
